items.title: How much does stacking independent layers actually cut breach odds?
items.description: Meridian effectively had one meaningful layer standing between an attacker's foothold and the database (a network route straight through); Castellan had several independent ones (segmentation, a scoped credential, per-request authorization, monitoring). If each layer has some independent chance of stopping an attacker on its own, the odds of getting through ALL of them multiply down fast. Drag the number of independent layers and each layer's own stop-rate to see why 2 layers at 60% each still leaves real exposure, while 5 layers at the same 60% each pushes the odds of a full breach into fractions of a percent.

params.name: numberOfLayers
params.label: Independent layers the attacker must get through

params.name: perLayerStopRate
params.label: Each layer's own chance of stopping the attacker

items.compute: const passRate = 1 - params.perLayerStopRate / 100; const breachProbability = Math.round(Math.pow(passRate, params.numberOfLayers) * 1000) / 10; return { breachProbability };

outputs.label: Chance the attacker gets all the way through

items.title: How many records does a service account's scope actually expose?
items.description: Castellan's `web_catalog_reader` account was granted SELECT on exactly 2 tables averaging 4,270 records each — products (8,200) and product_categories (340) — for the exact 8,540-record exposure the blast-radius calculator computed in L3. Drag how many tables a service account is granted against the database's average records per table to see how directly the grant decision, not the theft technique, determines the number.

params.name: tablesGranted
params.label: Tables granted to this service account

outputs.label: Records exposed if this credential is stolen
